title: ️Asking Questions, Designing Studies, and Making Inferences about Life on the Docks
text:
⁉️ Asking Questions About the World
Where do questions come from? When we learn the Scientific Method, we go through the typical observation -> question -> topic workflow, but, it’s not always clear how you start that process. Or how you form a hypothesis and conduct a well designed study.






TipReflection: How did you observe?



You all began to poke around the docks last week. What were things you saw that led you to questions or hypotheses?


Sometimes going from observation -> question is clear enough. But scientists also don’t blindly wander in the wilderness, seeing things and de novo turning it into a question or hypothesis. We have disciplines. Within those, we have topics and things we are interested in. It might be a system we’re interested in. For example, I’m endlessly fascinated by kelp forests. It might be a body of theory. I’m deeply curious about Foundation Species and how they shape the world around us.






TipReflection: What are your interests?



What ecosystems and bodies of theory/questions are you most interested in? Did any theory drive any of your initial thoughts - or are there biological theories that you find particularly interesting?


These interests guide us in how we conduct ourselves as scientists.
Once we have some observations of a system filtered through our interests and a priori knowledge, in order to turn it into a structured question and hypothesis, we need to think about how the world works. Well, but the ENTIRE world, but at least our corner of the world we want to study. Why?
There are three main domains of inquiry when taking data. Depending on our goals, each will guide us in how our study works. They are Description, Prediction, and Causal Understanding.







Description: Quantifying a measurement (how many mussels are here) or correlation (when we have more mussels do we have less algae?). Not positing WHY by positing WHAT is there.
Prediction: What might happen under a different set of conditions? This might seem like it requires causal knowledge, but, oddly, it doesn’t as long as you are within the current range of observed conditions (although if you do have causal knowledge, you can go outside of that).
Causal Understanding: If I were to change A, how would B change? If I took the sunlight away from a patch of the docks, how would algal cover change? This requires understanding the causal connections between two quantities, and it requires us to think about counterfactual scenarios (what would happen if…). To some extent, we’re always reaching for this level of understanding, but it’s hard. Nature loves to trick us!




Once we have a goal in mind, we can then ask a targeted and specific question.






TipReflection: What’s your question?



Based on this framing, what would you say your group’s question was? Where did it fall in the framing of the three goals of a scientific study?

section: 🗺️ Systems Thinking to Make a Map of Your World
text:
🗺️ Systems Thinking to Make a Map of Your World
To figure out how to answer our question - and perhaps even refine it a bit - we have to think about how we would apply our question to the world as it is. One we understand how we think the world works, we can establish the best study design possible.
To develop this understanding - regardless of which of the three areas of study we are pursuing - we must make a diagram of how we think our system works. In this diagram, we will think about the causal connections between the different elements of the system. I like to do this using something called a DAG or Directed Acyclic Graph. Don’t worry, these aren’t intimidating things - just box and arrow diagrams where the boxes or words represent things in the system and arrows represent causal relationships.
If we don’t know the specific natural history, we can rely on our knowledge of general principles of marine biology. For example, let’s say I was interested in how flow influenced tunicates on a dock. I might start by thinking about how flow influences filter feeders in general.

title: ️Asking Questions, Designing Studies, and Making Inferences about Life on the Docks
text:
🧫 Study Design
Great! Armed with the diagram above, we can ask a targeted question and design a study. For example, my initial question was: How does flow influence tunicate abundance? But now, I see that flow 1) has multiple pathways through which it might influence tunicates and 2) is confounded with other things we need to control for.
How might this influence our study design? Well, for one, it tells us that, because flow also unfluences Ulva, which influences tunicates, we’ll need to measure Ulva to control for it. It also raises questions about what we should use as a proxy for flow. Distance from end of dock - while important - seems like it might not be enough. Proximity to open water - that looks good. All of these suppose we can’t measure flow itself. We also see boat presence might influence flow.
That’s a lot! But, our diagram gives us a few strategies for success. First, assuming we don’t have a ‘flow meter’ - we can choose some predictor variables. In this case, let’s go with proximity to open water and distance from end of dock. We also have a response - tunicate cover. And, as we’ve noticed in the diagram, we need to control for Ulva cover. So we’ll need to measure that, too!






TipReflection: What did you measure?



Look back at your data and sampling plan. What did your group decide to measure? Why? Does it make sense given your now more up-to-date DAG of how the world works?


OK, now that we have some predictor variables, some things we’re going to control over, and a target response variable, we can apply some simple principles to make a well designed study.

You want to maximize the variation in your predictor conditions. A bigger range will give you more power to discern a difference.
You want to make sure, for every set of conditions, you have replication. Why? Well, look at it this way. If you went out and sampled one plot close to open water and one plot far away, and it just so happened that your plot close to the water had a boat recently crash into it (oops! What, was your professor practicing docking?) what you observe might have very little to do with the phenomenon you are studying. Better to take lots of measurements for each set of conditions to ensure you get an accurate estimate of its effect. Typically something like 5-7 replicates per unique set of conditions. If you have a continuous set of predictors, for each predictor you have, again, 5-7 (or better, 10) samples across the gradient of that predictor is a decent rule of thumb - more if one predictor can influence the other.







TipReflection: Your sampling design



While I pushed you to embrace some of the principles above, look at the diagram you made last week of your sampling design. Was it adequate? If you were to re-do the study, what would your sampling design look like. Work with your group to diagram out a new design.

🔂 Pivoting your data
Spreadsheets. What are they good for? Well. One thing. Data entry. By embracing the spreadsheet mindset, and thinking about wide or long data, you will a) become really good at designing field data collection sheets and b) develop good data entry practices quite quickly. I encourage it!
Now, what about the other things you can do in a spreadsheet? Honestly, I discourage use of their other functions unless you have a dire emergency. In my own work, I do all data analysis and figure making using programming. Why? To ensure that my entire workflow is repeatable and auditible. This is a cornerstone of good open and reproducible science.
But - that’s a whole different course! So, we’re going to use spreadsheets for a few tools they can give us. The first, is going from wide to long, and for that, let’s work through this handout together using this data. I’m going to teach you how to use something called Pivot Tables to move back and forth from wide to long.

🧠🐛❓ Would you like to know more?
For a good review of the early history of supply-side ecology, see Grosberg and Levitan (1992).
For more on global biogeography and its relationship to dispersal, see Álvarez-Noriega et al. (2020)
To understand the paleo-perspective on biogeography, see Jablonski and Sepkoski Jr. (1996), a classic.
To really get into the local adaptation side of marine invertebrates and how that relates to dispersal, see this excellent review by Sanford and Kelly (2011)
To learn more about currents in the Gulf of Maine and kelp dispersal biogeography, see Francolini et al. (2026)
The Cradle, Museum, Out of the Tropics model we discussed this week comes from Jablonski et al. 2006
The working group papser on the biogeography of extinction and risk comes from Finnegan et al. (2015) - the first time your prof was ever called a “Neoecologist”.

title: ️ Life on the Docks
text:
⚓️ Introduction
Floating docks represent a completely novel marine habitat. They are urban marine ecosystems at their most pure. They are full of invertebrate filter feeders – many non-native, algae, a wide variety of small arthropods (amphipods, isopods, etc.), and more. They are, however, a complex ecosystem. Docks are subjected to a number of environmental gradients – such as disturbance by boats, variation in light availability, differences in flow and more. The environmental conditions on a dock determine who can live there and how the community will ultimately function. Today we will explore this habitat and ask questions about what potential gradients in dock community composition we can observe. We will also generate hypotheses as to why and test them with structured sampling scheme.

title: ️ Life on the Docks

🧪 Methods

Lean over the edge and look at what species exist on the sides of the docks. Come up with a classification system based on the lowest taxonomic level you can master of who lives where.
Spend some time looking at the outer edge and back end of the dock. Look at the different sides of slips. See who lives on each side of a single walkway.
With your group, come up with a structured plan to sample the docks across some gradient in the environment. Discuss what information you need to record to characterize the differences of communities you observe on docks.
Record the taxonomic diversity of species and some measure of community composition.

title: How to Read a Scientific Paper
text:
Reading scientific papers for the first time is not a simple task. The language is stilted and strange. Jargon flies around casually. And once you get the gist of the paper, it’s difficult to hold on to where it fits in into the grand progression of ideas of science. Below are a few links to helpful resources on reading a paper.


First, though, here’s a mashup of some techniques that I have found helpful in the past as I began to read the literature. It’s a sort of altered reading order, rather than reading straight through, but it can help quite a bit as you begin to get a handle on the literature.



Read the abstract first. Really understand what the authors said they did and why it matters.


Read the last (or last two) paragraphs of the introduction, where the authors tell you what they tested and how in a brief summary. Write down their major questions.


Then read the methods. Sketch out each experiment, and above the sketch write the question the experiment was trying to answer or hypothesis it was testing.


Then read the figures. On each one, write the main point and draw all over it to make it clearer to you. Skim the results and see if they have any additional information other than statistical tests.


Read the discussion. Start with the first paragraph which should contain their main conclusions. Write down the answer to each of their major questions.


Ask yourself if you agree with what they say about their experiments. You may, or you may find some holes you want to note.


Last, read the introduction. All the way. Sit back and think about the big picture of why they did this work. Did the experiments, as you understood them, address or advance the field of knowledge they set out to advance?



But don’t just try the above. Check out these resources on reading papers and see what works best for you:


 


How to deconstruct a scientific paper – a WONDERFUL guide with an alternate reading technique to the above with a great infographic that I’ve put below


How to read and understand a scientific paper: a guide for non (or new!) -scientists

📑 Course Description
Focus: This course explores the diversity of biological and ecological processes that shape life in the oceans. It places special emphasis on marine life in New England, focusing on the interactions between humans and the sea. This focus leads to a greater understanding of the consequences of ongoing environmental changes witnessed in the 20th and 21st centuries.
How: Lectures, Paper Discussion, and Fieldwork for labs!


🎯 Learning Objectives

Understand how biological systems are structured and function within the world’s oceans.

Learn how to understand new scientific information and rapidly incorporate it into one’s knowledge of the goods and services produced by our oceans.
Gain an appreciation for how changes in the environment alter life in the sea and the concomitant indirect effects to human society.
Understand the historic, current, and future links between humans in New England and the ocean around us.

🌊 Additionally, for students in lab, we aim to have you:

Learn how experimental and observational data can and cannot be used to answer biological questions.
Learn how to conduct studies in coastal field environments.
Be able to conduct a small independent research project.
Be able to present results from a scientific study to colleagues.

title: 🗓️ Week 2 - Life in the Ocean

section: 🧠🐛❓ Would you like to know more?
text:
🧠🐛❓ Would you like to know more?
How did things evolve to be this way? You can find some answers in Antell and Saupe (2021)
If you’re a fish person, see Betancur-R et al. (2017) on some of the latest about the ways we organize bony fishes.
To understand more about algae and their relationship to land plants, see Bhattacharya and Medlin (1998)
If you’re an invert nerd and are also trying to follow all of the controversies there, see this review from Dunn et al. (2014) .

title: ️ Life on the Docks
text:
⚓️ Introduction
Floating docks represent a completely novel marine habitat. They are urban marine ecosystems at their most pure. They are full of invertebrate filter feeders – many non-native, algae, a wide variety of small arthropods (amphipods, isopods, etc.), and more. They are, however, a complex ecosystem. Docks are subjected to a number of environmental gradients – such as disturbance by boats, variation in light availability, differences in flow and more. The environmental conditions on a dock determine who can live there and how the community will ultimately function. Today we will explore this habitat and ask questions about what potential gradients in dock community composition we can observe. We will also generate hypotheses as to why and test them with structured sampling scheme.

title: ️ Life on the Docks
text:
🧪 Methods

Lean over the edge and look at what species exist on the sides of the docks. Come up with a classification system based on the lowest taxonomic level you can master of who lives where.
Spend some time looking at the outer edge and back end of the dock. Look at the different sides of slips. See who lives on each side of a single walkway.
With your group, come up with a structured plan to sample the docks across some gradient in the environment. Discuss what information you need to record to characterize the differences of communities you observe on docks.
Record the taxonomic diversity of species and some measure of community composition.
